newsitem.title: USA: Clinton lawyer asks sex-harassment case delay.
newsitem.headline: Clinton lawyer asks sex-harassment case delay.

text.p: President Bill Clinton asked the Supreme Court on Monday to give him temporary immunity from civil lawsuits and delay a sex-harassment case until after he leaves office in 2001.

But Clinton's accuser, former Arkansas state employee Paula Jones, asserted that "justice delayed is justice denied" and asked clearance to proceed with a $700,000 damage suit of momentous personal, political and constitutional import.

Lawyers for the two parties to an encounter that occurred in an Arkansas hotel room in 1991 argued their cases for one hour before the nine U.S. high court justices while Clinton went about presidential duties in the White House and Jones remained at home in California.
A ruling -- solely on the procedural issue of whether the case may procede immediately, not on its merits -- was expected before the Supreme Court session ends in June.

"We are saying we will give Miss Jones her day in court (but) let's not do it now," Clinton lawyer Robert Bennett said in arguing that vulnerability to civil suits for private conduct would open U.S. presidents to unacceptable burdens and diversions from attending to their high public duties.
Bennett, and Clinton, seek not only to postpone a trial in the politically embarrassing case but to delay any questioning of Clinton or any witnesses until he leaves office.
He is to be inaugurated to a second, four-year term next Monday and is due to step aside when his successor is sworn in on Jan. 20, 2001.
"What is unique here is the notion of taking the president of the United States of America ... and subjecting him to any court in the country," Bennett said.

Clinton's position was backed by a top Justice Department lawyer, Acting Solicitor General Walter Dellinger, who also said an incumbent president should not be distracted from the demands of the office by having to appear in court.

Jones claims that Clinton, then governor of Arkansas, had her summoned to a Little Rock hotel room during a government conference at the hotel in 1991 and, once the two were alone, exposed himself to her and asked her to perform oral sex.
Gilbert Davis, an attorney for Jones, said she should be able to press her lawsuit without further delay, arguing that Jones wants to restore her reputation as soon as possible.
Davis cited a number of potential problems if the case were delayed four years, saying Jones, Clinton or witnesses could die, the memories of witnesses could fade and documents could be lost.
"Justice delayed is justice denied," he told reporters on the courthouse steps later. "That is what the president would seek to have here -- to delay it, just push it off."
Clinton's lawyers declined to join the imprompute news conference.

The White House sidestepped questions about the hearing. "The issue before the court today is about the presidency and about the Constitution and you can read it in our briefs," presidential spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters.
The justices vigorously questioned all of the lawyers but gave no firm indication of how they would rule.
Davis estimated that a trial could last four or five days. But under questioning, he admitted a delay may be needed if it were to last two weeks.
Joseph Cammarata, another lawyer representing Jones, left open the possibility of negotiating a settlement out of court. "It's never too late to settle," he told reporters in answer to a question.

"Paula Jones has given us our marching orders, which are to get her her day in court, and by that she means she wants her good name and reputation back from Bill Clinton. He took it. She wants it and by God we're going to get it," he said.
But Cammarata also said that if Clinton apologised, expressed regret for his conduct and admitteed Jones did nothing wrong, then, "That gets close to where we need to be."
He told reporters: "It's never too late to settle."
Bennett, during the arguments, said Clinton "has spent substantial amounts of time on this case already."
But Justice Antonin Scalia asked why the high court should not wait until the president actually claims the case has taken up so much of his time that he could not appear in court or for questioning.

Scalia expressed scepticism about the Clinton argument that a president has a full-time job and should not be disturbed. "I don't find that terribly persuasive," he said, adding that presidents find time to play golf, for example.

Justice Anthony Kennedy also expressed concern that Clinton was free to work with his staff on the case while it is pending. "He is in the dominant position. It seems to me the imbalance here is very substantial," Kennedy said.
